ranking.rationale: Predominant degree awarded is a high-level institutional characteristic that strongly and stably shapes outcomes across domains, capturing broad differences in mission, student pipeline, and labor-market alignment without relying on geography, demographics, or likely domain-ID shortcuts.

Institution control (public/private nonprofit/for-profit) adds broad, semantically stable signal beyond degree type about pricing, selectivity, student mix, and outcomes, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than geography, race composition, or highly target-adjacent financial aid variables.

Admission rate adds strong institution-level selectivity signal that is broadly predictive across domains and complements degree type and control without directly encoding geography or demographic composition. It is more semantically stable than state/region, race-share, or income features and less redundant than closely related test-score variables at this stage.

Highest degree awarded adds broad institutional mission/academic-level signal beyond degree-granting status, control, and admissions selectivity. It is semantically tied to outcomes across domains and is more stable than geography, demographics, or highly redundant test-score features.

Student academic preparation is a strong, semantically stable predictor of college outcomes and adds substantial signal beyond institution type, degree level, and admit rate. SAT verbal midpoint captures selectivity and incoming student readiness without relying on geography, race composition, or other brittle domain-identifying shortcuts; it is also less redundant than rolled-up admission-rate variants and more broadly informative than niche program-mix features at this stage.

Engineering program share adds institution mission/academic mix information that is broadly predictive across domains and complements degree level, control, admissions rate, and verbal SAT without relying on geography, demographics, or likely domain identifiers. It is more stable for OOD generalization than state/region, race composition, or local socioeconomic proxies, and less redundant than additional test-score variants.

Undergraduate enrollment size adds broad, semantically stable signal about institutional scale and resources that complements degree level, control, selectivity, and program mix. It is less likely than geography, race composition, or student-demographic variables to act as a domain shortcut, and it is more generally informative than redundant test-score variants or narrow CIP shares.

Pell-share adds strong, broadly stable signal about student socioeconomic composition and institutional mission that complements selectivity, degree mix, control, and size. It is usually more transportable than geography, race-share, or state identifiers, and less redundant than additional SAT/ACT variants or closely related enrollment measures.

Average faculty salary adds strong institution-quality/resources signal that should generalize across domains and complements selectivity, degree mix, control, size, and student-aid composition already chosen. It is less likely than geography, race-composition, or student-origin demographics to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and is less redundant than additional test-score/admissions variants.

Instructional expenditures per FTE adds a strong, institution-level resource/quality signal that is broadly predictive across domains and complements selectivity, degree mix, size, Pell share, and faculty salary without relying on geography or student demographics. It is more stable and semantically tied to educational capacity than location, race-composition, or many student-background variables, and less redundant than additional test-score or admissions variants.

Part-time share adds strong institution- and student-body composition signal that is broadly predictive across domains and complements selectivity, size, resources, and Pell share already chosen. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than geography or race-composition variables, and less redundant than additional test-score or admissions variants.

In-state tuition adds strong, broadly stable signal about institutional price/market position and student sorting beyond selectivity, control, size, Pell share, and faculty resources. It is more semantically tied to college outcomes than geography or demographic-composition variables, and less brittle than state/region identifiers or student-race proxies.

Adds major-program composition beyond engineering, capturing a broadly stable labor-market and institutional-orientation signal with strong marginal value. It complements degree level, selectivity, size, tuition, and socioeconomic mix, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than geography, race composition, or student-background variables.

Adds robust academic-selectivity signal beyond verbal SAT alone and admission rate, improving coverage of student preparedness with relatively stable semantics across domains while avoiding direct geography, race, or other shortcut-heavy demographic features.

Adds broadly stable student-academic-preparation signal that complements SAT verbal/math and admission rate, while avoiding geography, race-composition, and other domain-identifier or shortcut features. ACT composite is semantically predictive across institutions and less redundant than location or demographic variables.

Adds broadly stable signal about student financing and economic vulnerability beyond Pell share, tuition, selectivity, and size. It is institution-level and semantically tied to student outcomes across domains, while being less of a direct geographic or demographic shortcut than race-composition, state, or region features.

Adds a strong, broadly stable affordability/low-income signal that complements PCTPELL and loan_ever while being less tied to geography or demographic composition than state, region, race-share, or zip-code census features. It is likely predictive across domains because Pell receipt reflects student financial need and institutional socioeconomic mix, which remain semantically relevant for college outcomes.

Adds broadly stable signal about student socioeconomic/educational background that is strongly relevant to college outcomes, while being less domain-specific and less likely to act as a geographic or demographic shortcut than state, region, race-composition, or zip-code composition features. It complements existing access/selectivity and aid variables without being as redundant as additional SAT/ACT or tuition variants.

Average family income adds strong, broadly stable socioeconomic signal beyond Pell, first-generation, and loan uptake. It captures students’ financial resources and opportunity context that should remain predictive across domains, while being less tied to explicit geography or institutional identifiers than state/region and less problematic than race-composition shortcuts.

Average age of entry adds strong, semantically stable signal about student composition and college type beyond selectivity, size, cost, and income already chosen. It is broadly predictive across domains, less likely than geography or race-share variables to act as a domain identifier, and more informative than redundant score/cost variants.

Health-program share adds strong, semantically stable signal about institutional program mix and labor-market orientation beyond existing degree level, selectivity, size, and business/engineering composition. It is more robust across domains than geography, race-composition, or other demographic/context proxies, and less redundant than additional SAT/ACT variants or duplicate cost measures.

Adds a broadly stable institutional quality/resource signal not yet captured by salary and instructional spending alone. The full-time faculty share reflects teaching capacity and student support in a way that should generalize across domains, while being less domain-identifying or shortcut-prone than geography, race composition, or highly redundant test-score/cost variants.

Overall undergraduate enrollment adds robust institutional scale beyond degree-seeking enrollment alone, complementing UGDS, selectivity, staffing, and tuition. Size is a stable structural predictor across domains, while avoiding more brittle geographic and demographic composition variables that may encode domain shifts or shortcuts.

Out-of-state tuition adds broad, semantically stable signal about institutional price/selectivity and market position beyond in-state tuition, control, admissions metrics, and size. It is less likely than geography, race-composition, or accreditor variables to act mainly as a domain identifier, and it complements the existing affordability/resources features with useful incremental variation.

Net tuition revenue per FTE adds institution-level financial capacity and pricing structure beyond sticker tuition, selectivity, staffing, and student SES already chosen. It is broadly tied to educational resources and outcomes in a way that should transfer across domains, while being less of a direct geographic or demographic shortcut than state, region, race-composition, or Census-derived neighborhood variables.

Adds a robust student-composition signal beyond the already selected part-time share measure: degree-/certificate-seeking part-time intensity is strongly tied to completion/earnings-related outcomes and remains semantically meaningful across domains, while being less brittle than geography, race-share, or other demographic shortcut features.

Adds robust signal about nontraditional student composition beyond mean age alone; this is typically strongly related to college outcomes and institutional type, while being more stable and less domain-specific than geography, race-share, or highly redundant test-score/cost variants.

Share of dependent students adds stable signal about student life stage and financial support structure that complements age_entry, agege24, first_gen, faminc, Pell, and part-time enrollment without relying on geography or race proxies. It is likely broadly predictive across domains because dependency status is tied to persistence and earnings-related outcomes through student composition rather than domain identity, and it offers more marginal value now than redundant test-score, tuition, or location features.

Average cost of attendance adds institution-level price/resource information that is broadly predictive and likely to transfer across domains, while being less tied to geography or demographic composition than state, region, race-share, or zip-code census variables. It complements already selected tuition and expenditure features by capturing the fuller student-facing cost structure with relatively stable semantics.

Carnegie size/setting adds broad institutional context that is usually predictive across domains and complements enrollment, degree level, selectivity, and cost already chosen. It captures stable differences in mission and campus environment without relying as directly on geography, race composition, or other brittle domain-identifying shortcuts.

Adds major-specific signal not yet covered: computer/information sciences share captures durable differences in program mix and labor-market orientation beyond existing health/business composition, while being less domain-identifying and less shortcut-prone than geography or race-composition features.

Median family income adds strong, semantically stable signal about student socioeconomic resources and likely outcomes beyond the already selected mean family income, Pell, dependency, and first-generation measures. It is less domain-identifying and less shortcut-prone than geography or race-composition variables, and offers more nonredundant value than additional test-score or program-share features.

Median household income adds strong, broadly stable socioeconomic signal beyond family-income and Pell proxies already selected, capturing local opportunity and affordability context that should generalize better than geography or race-composition features and is less redundant than additional test-score or program-share variables.

Adds a strong, semantically stable signal about students’ pre-college educational environment and socioeconomic advantage that complements family-income and first-generation variables already selected. It is likely more robust across domain shifts than geography, race-composition, or institution-identifier features, and less redundant than additional test-score or admissions variants.

Locale adds institution context that is broadly stable across domains and complements control, size, selectivity, tuition, and program mix without relying on state identifiers or demographic composition. It captures urban/suburban/rural differences that plausibly affect outcomes while being less brittle than region, race-share, or zip-code proxy features.

Distance-only status adds institution-structure information not yet captured by size, selectivity, tuition, or program mix, and it should remain broadly predictive across domains because fully online schools differ systematically in student composition, costs, and outcomes. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than state/region or race-composition features, and less redundant than additional SAT/ACT variants or nearby socioeconomic proxies already selected.

Adds likely nonlinear signal beyond age_entry and agege24 by capturing curvature in student age composition, which is a stable institutional characteristic tied to outcomes across domains. It is less likely than geography, race-share, or state identifiers to encode brittle domain shortcuts, and offers more marginal value than highly redundant admissions-score or cost variants already covered.

Adds broadly stable signal about student composition and life circumstances without relying on explicit geography or race. After income, age, dependency, Pell/loan, selectivity, size, and program mix are already covered, gender balance still provides complementary information about institution type and student outcomes, while being less domain-specific and less shortcut-prone than state/region, race-share, HBCU, or census demographic features.

Poverty rate adds broad socioeconomic context that is likely to remain predictive across domain shifts and complements already selected family-income, Pell, and education measures without relying on direct racial composition, geography identifiers, or highly redundant test-score/program proxies.

Local unemployment rate adds broadly stable socioeconomic context that can affect college outcomes and student behavior across domains, while being less direct demographic shortcutting than race-composition features and less domain-identifying than state/region. It is also complementary to already selected income, poverty, and education-context variables.

Adds a broadly stable signal about nontraditional student composition that is not yet captured by age, dependency, or part-time share alone. It can improve prediction through student life-stage and enrollment-intensity effects while avoiding stronger domain-ID and demographic-shortcut risks than state, region, race-share, or accreditor variables.

Adds a robust admissions-selectivity signal closely related to outcomes but still semantically stable across domains; it complements ADM_RATE by covering multi-campus/rolled-up institutions, while remaining safer for OOD generalization than geography, race-composition, or other demographic shortcut features.

Net price adds strong institution-level affordability signal beyond sticker tuition and cost already selected, and should remain semantically predictive across domains without relying on explicit geography or racial composition. It captures realized student cost burden more directly than tuition alone and is less likely than demographic-share features to encode brittle domain shortcuts.

Education program mix adds institution-level signal about labor-market orientation and completion/earnings patterns that should transfer across domains. It complements existing broad program features without relying on geography, race composition, or other likely domain-identifying shortcuts.

Adds institution-level academic preparedness signal that is likely stable across domains and complementary to SAT/ACT composite and math/verbal measures already selected; more robust than geography, race-composition, or other demographic proxies, and less redundant than many remaining program-share features.

Adds another broadly stable academic-preparedness signal that complements SAT/ACT composite and verbal scores already selected. ACT math is semantically tied to student readiness and outcomes across domains, while being less likely than geography, race-composition, or state identifiers to encode brittle domain shifts or shortcut information.

Urbanization level adds institution-context signal that is plausibly stable across domains and complements LOCALE with finer granularity, affecting access, commuting, labor markets, and student mix without relying as directly on state/region identifiers or sensitive demographic composition.

Adds a broadly stable academic-program signal via biological/biomedical concentration that complements already selected STEM/business/health mixes. Program mix is institution-semantic and likely to transfer across domains better than geography, race-composition, or other demographic/location proxies, while offering more marginal information than highly redundant test-score or cost variants.

Adds a semantically stable academic-program signal not yet covered: math/stat intensity often predicts outcomes through rigor, selectivity, and labor-market alignment, while being less tied to geography or demographic shortcuts than race-composition, state, or region features. It is also less redundant with the already selected business, health, engineering, education, and communications program shares.

Adds broad socioeconomic/context signal from students’ home neighborhoods that is plausibly stable across domains and complementary to income, poverty, and parental-education features already chosen. It is less direct as an institutional/domain identifier than state/region and likely offers more marginal value now than additional highly redundant test-score or major-share variables, while avoiding the stronger shortcut risk of institution racial-composition features.

Adds stable socioeconomic context beyond family-income and local BA-rate features already chosen: professional-degree share captures neighborhood educational capital and opportunity structure that should generalize across domains, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region and less problematic than race-composition variables.

Adds institution-level academic preparedness signal beyond verbal/math and admissions selectivity already chosen; SAT writing is relatively stable across domains and less likely than geography or race-composition variables to encode domain membership or demographic shortcuts.

Number of branch campuses adds institution-structure signal that is plausibly stable across domains and complementary to control, degree level, size, and main-campus status. It can capture multi-campus systems and operational complexity without relying as directly on geography or demographic composition as state/region or race-share features, making it a stronger OOD-safe next choice.

Main-campus status adds institution-structure information that should generalize across domains and complements size, branch count, degree level, and pricing without relying on geography or demographic composition. It is likely more stable and less shortcut-prone than state/region, race-share, or niche program-share candidates, while still capturing meaningful differences in resources, student services, and outcomes.

Psychology program share adds institution-level academic mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. It can capture meaningful differences in student pathways and outcomes beyond selectivity, cost, and demographics, while avoiding brittle geographic identifiers and sensitive race-composition shortcuts.

Adds a strong, semantically meaningful institutional-type signal not yet captured by degree level, control, selectivity, costs, size, or program mix. It can affect student support structures and outcomes in a way that should remain predictive across domains, while being less like a pure geographic/domain identifier than state or region and less directly a demographic shortcut than detailed racial composition features.

Accreditor adds institution-level quality/governance signal that can remain predictive across domains and is less direct domain-ID leakage than state/region. It complements control, degree level, selectivity, spending, and program mix already chosen, while avoiding the stronger shortcut risk of race-composition and geography features.

Adds a meaningful, relatively stable student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected academic, cost, and socioeconomic variables. Veteran share can capture nontraditional enrollment patterns and institutional mission in a way that should generalize better than state/region identifiers or race-composition features, while offering less redundancy than additional test-score or program-share variables.

Adds institution program mix signal that is likely to generalize across domains and complements already selected STEM/health/business shares. Agriculture share captures a distinct vocational/rural mission linked to outcomes without relying on explicit geography, state, or race composition, making it a stronger stable addition than remaining demographic or regional candidates.

Adds institution-level student composition signal that is often strongly predictive in College Scorecard while remaining more semantically tied to campus context than pure geography. It complements already selected socioeconomic variables, but is preferable to state/region identifiers and student-zip demographic proxies, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or brittle shortcuts.

Adds institution-level student composition signal not yet covered by the selected set. Relative to broader geography features like state/region, this is less of a direct domain identifier, and compared with zip-code race proxies it is more tied to the college’s actual enrolled population. It complements existing socioeconomic variables and HBCU/white-share features with meaningful, semantically stable information about institutional context while avoiding the strongest leakage and location-shortcut candidates.

Adds broad student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected set. Hispanic enrollment share is often stably associated with institutional mission, support needs, and outcomes beyond existing size, selectivity, cost, and white/black composition features. It is less like a direct geographic domain label than state/region and likely offers more marginal value than additional narrow program-share variables or redundant race encodings.

Adds meaningful student-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, helping capture institution mix and selectivity in a way that can remain predictive across domains. It is less like a direct geographic domain identifier than state/region and offers more marginal value than redundant ACT-writing or niche program-share variables.

Adds stable net-price/cost information for program-year institutions, complementing existing tuition and cost variables while covering schools not well represented by academic-year pricing fields. It is more semantically tied to affordability and student outcomes than geography or additional race-share variables, and offers broader marginal value than another highly redundant test-score or major-share feature.

Program-year tuition adds institution-level price information not yet covered by in/out-state tuition, especially for certificate and nontraditional schools. It is semantically tied to affordability and student outcomes across domains, while being less like a direct geographic/domain identifier than state or region and less shortcut-prone than adding more race-composition variables.

Adds broad academic-program composition signal that is likely stable across domains and complementary to already selected STEM/business/health fields; liberal-arts share captures institutional mission and student mix without relying on brittle geography or demographic shortcut variables.

Adds broad academic-program composition signal that is likely to generalize across domains and complements already selected STEM/business/health fields. Compared with state/region and race-composition variables, it is less likely to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and it is more semantically stable than niche or redundant score features.

Adds broad academic-program composition signal that is likely to remain predictive across domains and complements already selected CIP fields without relying on geography or demographic shortcuts; social-science share can capture institution mission and labor-market orientation with relatively stable semantics.

Adds a broadly stable signal about institutional program mix via engineering-technology emphasis, complementing existing degree-level, selectivity, cost, and major-share features without relying on geography or demographic composition. It is likely more transportable across domains than state/region or additional race-share variables, and less redundant than ACT writing or many niche CIP categories.

Adds broad academic-program composition signal not yet covered by the selected CIP mix. Physical sciences share is semantically tied to institutional mission, selectivity, and labor-market returns in a way that should transfer across domains, while being less direct as a geographic or demographic shortcut than state/region or additional race-composition variables.

Adds a still-missing, semantically meaningful program-mix signal: protective services/public safety specialization can materially affect student outcomes and institutional profile beyond the already selected broad academics, costs, selectivity, and other CIP shares. It is more stable across domains than geography features and less likely to act as a demographic or domain shortcut than additional race-composition variables.

Adds broadly stable socioeconomic context through students’ origin communities without relying on direct state/region identifiers. It complements existing income, poverty, unemployment, and race-composition variables with an immigration/assimilation signal that can affect college outcomes and institutional fit, while being less brittle than STABBR/region and less shortcut-prone than adding more campus racial-share features.

Adds broad student-neighborhood composition signal that can matter for outcomes beyond institution-level controls, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region and less redundant than more race-share variants or niche program-share fields.

Adds useful socioeconomic/context signal from students’ home ZIPs that can remain predictive across domains, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/region and less redundant than more race-share variants already covered by campus composition and pct_white/pct_black.

Adds broad academic-program mix signal that is likely to generalize across domains and complements already selected CIP fields. Multi/interdisciplinary share captures institution mission and student pathways without relying on brittle geography or direct demographic identifiers, while remaining less redundant than ACT writing or additional race-share variants.

Adds student academic preparation signal that is usually robust across domains and complements already selected SAT/ACT composite/English/math measures. It is more semantically tied to outcomes than remaining geography features, and less likely than state/region or additional race-share variables to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Adds student-origin neighborhood composition signal not yet covered: it complements income, poverty, parental education, and campus racial mix with a distinct pre-college context feature that can remain predictive across domains. It is likely more stable and less domain-identifying than state/region, and offers more marginal value than the remaining highly sparse or redundant program-share and race-share variables.

Adds semantically meaningful program-mix signal not yet covered: public administration/social service concentration can stably predict student outcomes and institutional profile across domains. It is less likely than state/region features to encode domain identity, and offers more marginal value than remaining race-share variants, which are redundant with already selected demographic composition features and risk shortcutting.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is likely to generalize across domains and is less redundant than remaining options. A natural-resources/conservation share captures a distinctive academic orientation not yet covered by the selected CIP fields, while avoiding brittle geographic identifiers like state/region and avoiding additional demographic composition variables that are more likely to encode domain shifts or shortcuts.

Adds broad academic-program mix signal not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. Visual/performing arts share is institution-level and semantically tied to college type, selectivity, costs, and student outcomes, while being less like a direct geographic/domain identifier than state or region and less redundant than many race-share variants already partly captured.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is likely to generalize across domains and is less redundant than remaining options. A distinct academic specialization share can improve prediction beyond already selected broad selectivity, cost, and existing CIP fields, while avoiding brittle geographic identifiers like state/region and avoiding additional demographic composition variables that risk shortcutting or duplicating already selected race-share features.

Adds institution program mix signal via science-technician orientation, which can stably affect outcomes beyond selectivity, cost, and already chosen CIP fields. It is less likely than state/region to encode domain identity and less redundant than additional race-share variables already well covered.

Adds broadly stable signal about institutional academic/program mix that is not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. Communication/journalism concentration can meaningfully affect outcomes across domains, while being less likely than state/region features to encode the benchmark’s domain split directly and less redundant than additional race-share variables already proxied by selected demographics.

Adds a broadly meaningful, institution-level signal about international student share that can remain predictive across domains and complements existing selectivity, cost, and program-mix features. It is less direct as a geographic/domain identifier than state or region, and likely offers more stable marginal value than redundant race-share variants or niche CIP fields.

Adds institution-level international-student composition, which can stably capture selectivity, mission, and labor-market orientation beyond the already selected academic, cost, and broad demographic features. It is more semantically predictive and less direct as a geographic/domain identifier than state or region, and likely more informative than the remaining niche program-share variables or highly redundant race-share variants.

Adds a semantically meaningful program-mix signal (legal professions) that can stably affect outcomes through earnings/completion pathways and is less likely than state/region or additional race-share variables to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts. It is also less redundant than many remaining CIP fields because major mix is already useful in this dataset and legal-program concentration captures a distinct institutional profile not yet covered by the selected CIP features.

Adds a still-useful enrollment-composition signal not yet directly covered in the undergraduate race-share variables, while being less overtly geographic/domain-identifying than state or region. It complements existing institutional selectivity, cost, program mix, and socioeconomic features with moderate marginal value; remaining candidates are mostly redundant race-share variants, niche program shares, or stronger domain shortcuts.

Adds modest but still stable signal about institutional reporting quality and student composition via the share of undergraduates with unknown race, which can proxy administrative capacity and enrollment mix without relying as directly on geography as state/region or adding highly redundant race-share variants already covered by selected demographic features.

Adds a relatively stable student-composition signal via non-Hispanic white undergraduate share, complementing already selected aggregate race shares and degree-seeking composition variables while avoiding stronger domain-ID leakage from state/region. It is less redundant than the remaining PCIP niche programs and more broadly predictive of institutional context than tiny-share race categories.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is likely to generalize across domains and is less redundant than remaining options. Geographic identifiers like state/region are strong domain markers, and remaining race-share variables are mostly redundant or shortcut-prone given many demographic features already selected.

Adds broadly stable signal about academic program mix via foreign-language/liberal-arts orientation, which can affect outcomes beyond already selected STEM/business/health fields. It is less likely than state/region or fine-grained race-share variables to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts, and offers more marginal value than highly sparse vocational/religious specialty fields.

Adds meaningful program-mix signal not yet covered: theology/religious-vocation specialization can strongly shape institutional mission, student body, pricing, and outcomes, while being more semantically stable across domains than geography features like state/region and less redundant than remaining race-share variants or tiny CIP categories.

Adds institution program-mix signal not yet covered by the selected CIP fields: construction-trades share is a strong, semantically stable indicator of vocational orientation, labor-market pathway, and student composition. It should generalize better across domains than geography features like state/region and is less redundant than remaining race-share variants or duplicate ethnicity encodings.

Adds a remaining student-composition signal with some stable socioeconomic/selection information while being less redundant than state/region and less brittle than legacy race-code duplicates. Most other candidates are either weak niche program shares, direct geographic domain identifiers, or near-duplicates of already selected demographic proportions.

Adds a still-unused academic-program composition signal that can matter for outcomes while being less likely than geography features to encode domain identity. It is more complementary than the remaining race-share variables, many of which are redundant with already selected demographic composition features or are legacy duplicates.

Adds a still-unused academic-program mix signal that is institution-semantic and likely to transfer across domains better than geography features or redundant race-share variants. It complements the many existing PCIP fields without relying on state/region identifiers or demographic shortcuts.

Adds a still-unused program-mix signal with plausible stable value: mechanic/repair technologies captures vocational orientation and labor-market pathway differences not fully covered by the already selected major-share features. It is more semantically tied to institution offerings than geography features like state/region and less redundant or shortcut-prone than additional race-composition variants.

Adds institution-level academic program mix not yet covered by the selected CIP fields, and is more likely to reflect stable educational orientation than geography-coded variables like state/region. It should provide incremental signal beyond selectivity, size, cost, and existing program shares while avoiding direct domain identifiers and minimizing demographic shortcut risk.

Adds a small but still semantically meaningful enrollment-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features. It is more institution-level and stable than state/region identifiers, less redundant than legacy duplicate race variables, and likely offers better marginal value than very sparse niche program-share fields.

Adds institution mission signal via humanities/religion program mix, which can stably affect outcomes beyond already selected size, selectivity, cost, and major-composition features. It is less likely than state/region or redundant race-share variables to encode domain identity or demographic shortcuts.

Adds institution program-mix signal that can generalize across domains and is less likely to act as a direct geographic/domain identifier than state or region. Most remaining candidates are either redundant race-share variants of already selected enrollment composition features or very sparse niche CIP codes with weaker marginal value.

Among remaining options, this program-mix feature is the strongest likely to add institution-level signal that can generalize across domains. Most other candidates are state/region identifiers or redundant race-share variants already covered by selected demographics, which are more likely to encode domain shifts or duplicate existing information. Precision-production share can capture vocational/technical orientation not yet well represented and should remain semantically predictive out of domain.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not yet covered by the selected CIP fields. It is more semantically tied to college offerings than geography features like state/region, and less redundant or shortcut-prone than the remaining race-share variants, which largely duplicate already selected demographic composition variables.

Adds a small but plausibly stable institutional signal via academic program mix, while most remaining options are weaker or redundant race-share variants already covered by selected demographics, and state/region are likely domain identifiers that hurt OOD generalization.

Adds institution program-mix signal that is plausibly stable across domains and not yet covered by selected CIP fields. Transportation/materials-moving can capture vocational and career-oriented school specialization linked to outcomes, while remaining less direct as a geographic/domain identifier than state or region and less redundant than race-share variants already represented.

Adds a still-unused academic-program composition signal, which can capture institution mission and labor-market orientation in a way that is more semantically tied to outcomes than geography features like state/region. The remaining race-share candidates are mostly redundant with already selected enrollment composition variables, while state/region are likely to encode domain identity and hurt OOD robustness.

Adds a small but still semantically meaningful enrollment-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, while avoiding the stronger domain-identifier risk of state/region and the near-duplicate redundancy of the old/non-Hispanic race-share variants already represented.

Adds a small but still potentially useful institution-level composition/measurement signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, while avoiding the stronger domain-identifier risk of state/region. The remaining race-share candidates are mostly redundant with already selected UGDS/UG composition variables, and state/region are more likely to encode brittle geographic shifts than stable causal structure.

Adds a broadly predictive enrollment-composition signal not yet explicitly captured in the non-Hispanic coding, and is more useful than the remaining race-share variants because white share often summarizes institutional selectivity, mission, and peer composition. It is somewhat shortcut-prone, but still offers the best marginal value among the remaining candidates; state/region are stronger domain identifiers, and the other candidates are mostly redundant with already selected race-share features.

Adds a still-meaningful enrollment-composition signal not fully captured by existing race-share features, while avoiding the stronger domain-identifier risk of state/region. It is more useful than the legacy duplicate race variables because the dataset already includes newer UGDS race shares, and this non-Hispanic black share can refine student-body composition with less redundancy than the old aggregated categories.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal not yet covered: Asian/Pacific Islander share among degree-seeking undergraduates. This can capture stable differences in student mix and institutional mission beyond the already selected race-share features, while avoiding the stronger domain-identifier risk of state/region. It is also less redundant than the older or non-degree-seeking variants among the remaining candidates.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal with some stable socioeconomic relevance, while avoiding stronger domain-identifier features like state/region. It is partly redundant with existing race-share variables, but still offers more marginal value than the other leftover demographic duplicates.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal not yet directly covered: undergraduate black non-Hispanic share can capture institution/student-body composition with some stable association to outcomes, while being less domain-identifying than state or region. The other candidates are either redundant legacy race-share variants or stronger geographic/domain indicators likely to hurt OOD robustness.

Adds a remaining enrollment-composition signal not yet covered by the selected race-share features, with likely modest but stable predictive value. It is less directly a geographic/domain identifier than state or region, and less redundant/obsolete than the older AIAN variants.

Adds a small amount of institution/student-composition signal not yet fully covered, while being less likely than state or region to act as a direct domain identifier. It is partly redundant with existing race-share features, but still offers more stable marginal value than geographic identifiers; the remaining alternative is even more redundant.

Adds a small amount of residual student-composition signal, while the remaining geographic features are more likely to act as domain identifiers and hurt out-of-distribution generalization. It is also less redundant than state/region after many institutional and demographic variables are already included.
